newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai Metal Exchange seen major trading floor.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai Metal Exchange seen major trading floor.

text.p: Shanghai Metal Exchange (SHME) is well on the way to achieving its aim of becoming a major metals trading floor in Asia, exchange chairman Zhou Xiaohong said on Wednesday.
Speaking at the fifth birthday celebrations of the exchange, Zhou said 88 million tonnes of copper worth 1,900 billion yuan had been traded on the exchange in the 1,102 trading days since it opened.
This put it behind the London Metal Exchange (LME) and the New York Commodities Exchange in terms of volume, she said, without giving further details.

David Waite, the director of business development for London broking firm Rudolph Wolff said the SHME had matured in its five years and was a contender, along with the Tokyo Commodities Exchange, for Asian leadership as a metals trading floor.
Passing its fifth birthday was for the SHMA "one of many milestones in the development of what will be one of the world's most important metals futures exchanges," he said.
Total traded volume of copper and aluminium on the SHME in 1996 was 10.74 million tonnes worth a total of 230.5 billion yuan, the exchange's 1996 anual report shows.
Of that total, 10.51 million tonnes was copper worth 226.5 billion yuan, and 213,800 tonnes was aluminium worth 3.2 billion yuan, the report shows.
Zhou said the exchange had grown in five years from 43 founding members to 120 member companies and 3,400 clients.

The introduction in recent years of risk control and liquidation disclosure measures meant the Shanghai exchange's futures prices, the Chinese domestic cash price and the international market price were now similar and largely reflected market fundamentals, she said.
Chinese domestic base metals prices were now largely a reflection of quotations on the exchange, she said.
Some of China's major copper producers, including the Jiangxi and Tongling smelters, now hedged their product on the exchange as the basis of their business, she said.
About 20 percent of the metal held in exchange warehouses was hedged on the exchange, she said.
